Neonates of the monocled cobra emerge from parchment-shelled eggs after an incubation period that typically lasts 57 days [ab = 57 days] when eggs are maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], though hatching has been observed to occur anywhere from 50 to 73 days depending on slight thermal fluctuations. This incubation duration is comparable to that of other large elapids such as the king cobra (Ophiophagus hannah) and reflects the energetic demands of embryonic development within a cleidoic egg, where the yolk-laden embryo relies entirely on endogenous reserves until eclosion. At the moment of eclosion, these hatchlings exhibit a snout-vent length of approximately 27.5 cm [Lb = approximately 27.5 cm], a size that reflects the substantial yolk reserves invested by the gravid female and which places the newborn cobra at a competitive advantage for securing small prey items shortly after the onset of exogenous feeding, a critical transition that follows the complete absorption of internal yolk stores. Hatchlings are immediately capable of defensive displays and possess functional venom glands, traits that reduce predation risk during the vulnerable early post-hatching period, and their relatively large size at birth likely enhances their ability to capture suitable prey items, including small amphibians and reptiles, during the first weeks of independent life.

As individuals transition through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, growth proceeds steadily under favorable thermal regimes. Sexual maturation, marked by the attainment of gonadal activation and the ability to produce viable gametes, is closely tied to a threshold body size rather than a strict chronological age. Field studies indicate that the onset of puberty occurs once a snake reaches a snout-vent length of approximately 100 cm [Lp = approximately 100 cm], a size that typically corresponds to an age of several years in wild populations. Reaching this developmental milestone enables a young cobra to begin participating in the reproductive population, although competition with larger, more experienced individuals may delay actual breeding until the animal achieves a more dominant social position. The energetic demands of reaching this size threshold are considerable, requiring consistent access to prey and suitable basking sites to maintain optimal body temperatures for digestion and growth.

Size dimorphism is a notable feature of the monocled cobra's life history, with females attaining a substantially larger ultimate body size than males. The maximum recorded snout-vent length for adult females reaches 165 cm [Li = 165 cm], whereas males typically achieve a maximum snout-vent length of 145 cm [Li = 145 cm]. This difference in asymptotic size is thought to reflect the selective pressures associated with fecundity, as larger females can produce larger clutches and potentially larger eggs, thereby enhancing offspring survival. Males, by contrast, may benefit from a more slender, agile body form that facilitates mate searching and combat with rival males during the breeding season. The attainment of these maximum lengths occurs slowly over many years of adult life, with growth rates decelerating markedly after the onset of sexual maturity as resources are increasingly directed toward reproductive functions rather than somatic expansion.

Reproductive output in the monocled cobra is substantial, though it is constrained by the energetic costs of egg production and the need for the female to maintain her own body condition. Under controlled laboratory conditions maintained at 25 °C [T = 25 °C], a gravid female with a snout-vent length of 136.7 cm produces a clutch of approximately 23 eggs [N_R_i = a clutch of approximately 23 eggs]. The frequency of reproductive events is variable, however, with individual females typically producing a single clutch every 1 to 3 years [F_R_i = single clutch every 1 to 3 years], a pattern that reflects the considerable energy investment required for vitellogenesis and the subsequent period of post-oviposition recovery. This relatively slow reproductive tempo, combined with a moderate clutch size, suggests a life-history strategy that prioritizes offspring quality and maternal survival over the production of numerous, small clutches in quick succession.

Longevity data for the monocled cobra, derived from captive populations maintained at a constant temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], indicate that the maximum lifespan recorded for this species is approximately 24.5 years [am = approximately 24.5 years]. This surprisingly long lifespan, unusual among elapids of comparable body size, likely represents the upper bound of physiological potential achieved under conditions of consistent food availability and the absence of predation pressure or disease. In natural settings, most individuals probably succumb to ecological mortality factors—including predation by larger snakes, birds of prey, and mongooses, as well as habitat loss and human persecution—well before reaching such an advanced age. The ability to persist for over two decades nonetheless underscores a life-history strategy that emphasizes iteroparity and reproductive longevity, allowing females to produce multiple clutches across a protracted adult lifespan and thereby maximize lifetime reproductive success.
